questions.q: Define monosaccharide and give two examples.
questions.a: A monosaccharide is a carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolyzed to a simpler polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone. Examples: glucose, fructose. A wrong answer (e.g., naming sucrose as a monosaccharide) reveals confusion between hydrolysis behavior and taste/sweetness.

questions.q: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar while maltose is a reducing sugar? Explain in terms of glycosidic linkage.
questions.a: Sucrose has a glycosidic bond between the anomeric carbons of glucose (C1) and fructose (C2), so neither monosaccharide unit has a free carbonyl group. Maltose has a C1–C4 glycosidic linkage leaving the anomeric carbon (C1) of the second glucose free, allowing it to open to an aldehyde and reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagent. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are reducing") shows misunderstanding of anomeric carbon involvement.

questions.q: A carbohydrate on hydrolysis gives two molecules of glucose only. Identify the carbohydrate and write its hydrolysis reaction. Is it reducing or non-reducing?
questions.a: The carbohydrate is maltose. Hydrolysis: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → 2 C₆H₁₂O₆. It is a reducing sugar because the second glucose unit retains a free anomeric carbon (C1) that can form an aldehyde group. A wrong answer (e.g., sucrose) shows inability to link hydrolysis products to structure and reducing property.

questions.q: Compare starch and cellulose in terms of monomer, glycosidic linkage, and biological function. Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
questions.a: Both are polymers of glucose. Starch: α-D-glucose with α-1,4 (amylose) and α-1,6 (amylopectin) linkages; functions as energy storage in plants. Cellulose: β-D-glucose with β-1,4 linkages; functions as structural material in plant cell walls. Humans produce amylase that hydrolyzes α-glycosidic bonds but lack cellulase for β-glycosidic bonds. A wrong answer (e.g., "same linkage") shows lack of stereochemical understanding.

questions.q: A student claims: "All disaccharides are reducing sugars because they have a free anomeric carbon." Evaluate this statement with two counterexamples.
questions.a: The statement is false. Sucrose (α-D-glucose–β-D-fructose, C1–C2 linkage) and trehalose (α,α-1,1 linkage) are non-reducing disaccharides because both anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond. Only disaccharides with one free anomeric carbon (maltose, lactose) are reducing. A wrong evaluation shows overgeneralization without checking linkage type.

questions.q: Design a simple laboratory test to distinguish between glucose, sucrose, and starch using only Benedict's reagent and iodine solution. Explain expected observations.
questions.a: Benedict's test: glucose (reducing) gives brick-red precipitate; sucrose (non-reducing) gives no precipitate unless hydrolyzed first; starch (polysaccharide) gives no precipitate. Iodine test: starch gives blue-black complex; glucose and sucrose give no color. A poor answer misses the need for acid hydrolysis of sucrose before Benedict's test or confuses Benedict's with Fehling's reagent.
